title: Surface Areas and Volumes of Solids
prerequisites: Area of a rectangle, triangle and circle.
Idea of three-dimensional shapes and their nets.
Ability to handle squares, cubes and square roots.

topics.title: Cuboid, Cube and Cylinder
topics.quick_summary: Surface area is the area of the outer covering of a solid and volume is the space it occupies; for prisms and cylinders volume is simply base area times height.
topics.real_life: The paper needed to wrap a gift box is its surface area, while the amount it can hold is its volume — two different questions about the same box.

detailed.definition: Total surface area is the area of all the faces of a solid. Lateral or curved surface area excludes the top and bottom faces. Volume is the space enclosed by the solid.
detailed.key_idea: For any prism or cylinder, volume = base area × height. Learning this one principle replaces three separate volume formulas.
detailed.working_principle: The curved surface of a cylinder unrolls into a rectangle of width 2πr and height h, which is exactly why its curved surface area is 2πrh.
applications: Cost of painting a wall uses surface area; capacity of a tank uses volume.
A hollow cylinder such as a pipe requires both the inner and outer radii.

points: Cuboid: TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), Volume = lbh, diagonal = √(l² + b² + h²).
Cube: TSA = 6a², Volume = a³, diagonal = a√3.
Cylinder: CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h), Volume = πr²h.
Lateral surface area of a cuboid = 2h(l + b), excluding top and bottom.
All dimensions must be converted to the same unit before substituting.
mistakes: Using total surface area where only the curved or lateral area is needed (e.g. painting only the walls).
Mixing units — length in metres and radius in centimetres.
Using the diameter in place of the radius in a cylinder formula.
topics.memory_hook: 'Volume = base area × height' for every prism and cylinder — one rule, three solids.
topics.advanced: Cavalieri's principle explains why a slanted stack of coins has the same volume as a straight one: equal cross-sections at every height give equal volume, regardless of how the solid leans.

formulas.name: Cuboid and Cube
formulas.formula: Cuboid: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl);  Cube: V = a³, TSA = 6a²
formulas.variables: l, b, h = length, breadth, height; a = edge of the cube.
formulas.when_to_use: For boxes, rooms, tanks, bricks and any rectangular solid.
formulas.common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor 2 in the total surface area of a cuboid.
formulas.shortcut: Diagonal of a cuboid = √(l²+b²+h²); of a cube = a√3.

formulas.name: Cylinder
formulas.variables: r = radius of the base, h = height of the cylinder.
formulas.when_to_use: For pipes, tanks, rollers, cans and drums.
formulas.common_mistakes: Substituting the diameter for r, which quadruples the volume.
formulas.shortcut: A roller covers CSA per revolution; multiply by the number of revolutions for area covered.

topics.title: Cone, Sphere and Hemisphere
topics.quick_summary: A cone has one third the volume of a cylinder on the same base and height, and a sphere has volume (4/3)πr³ with surface area 4πr².
topics.real_life: An ice cream cone holds exactly one third of what a cylindrical cup of the same width and height would hold — which is why it looks bigger than it is.

detailed.definition: The slant height l of a cone is the distance from the apex to any point on the edge of the base, and satisfies l² = r² + h². A hemisphere is half of a sphere.
detailed.key_idea: The cone's curved surface uses the slant height l, while its volume uses the vertical height h. Substituting one for the other is the most frequent error in this chapter.
detailed.working_principle: For combined solids, add the curved surfaces of the parts that remain exposed and ignore the joined faces. Volumes always add directly.
applications: A cone, hemisphere and cylinder of the same radius and height have volumes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
A sphere's surface area equals the curved surface of the cylinder that just encloses it.
Melting and recasting problems keep volume constant while shape changes.

points: Cone: l² = r² + h², CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l + r), V = (1/3)πr²h.
Cone : hemisphere : cylinder volumes on the same base and height = 1 : 2 : 3.
In recasting problems, volume is conserved even though surface area changes.
mistakes: Using slant height l in the volume formula instead of vertical height h.
Taking the total surface area of a hemisphere as 2πr² and forgetting the flat circular face.
Adding the surface areas of joined faces in a combined solid.
topics.memory_hook: 'Cone is a third of a cylinder, sphere is two thirds of it' — and 'l for curved, h for volume'.
topics.advanced: Archimedes proved that a sphere has two thirds the volume and two thirds the total surface area of its circumscribing cylinder, and asked for that figure to be carved on his tomb — he considered it his finest result.

formulas.name: Cone
formulas.formula: l = √(r² + h²),  CSA = πrl,  TSA = πr(l + r),  V = (1/3)πr²h
formulas.variables: r = base radius, h = vertical height, l = slant height.
formulas.when_to_use: For conical tents, funnels, heaps of grain and ice-cream cones.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using l in the volume formula, or h in the curved surface area formula.
formulas.shortcut: Canvas needed for a conical tent is the curved surface area only.

formulas.name: Sphere and Hemisphere
formulas.formula: Sphere: SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³;  Hemisphere: CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², V = (2/3)πr³
formulas.when_to_use: For balls, domes, bowls and spherical tanks.
formulas.common_mistakes: Omitting the flat face when the total surface area of a hemisphere is required.
